Bragg spot intensity explorer

Cubic insulin (I2₁3, a = 78.1 Å) on a simulated DECTRIS EIGER2 XE 16M. Move a parameter to see which term of the Darwin/Holton–Frankel equation it changes, and how the diffraction image changes with it.

Ispot= Ibeam  re2  P  L  A  λ3  Vxtal  |F|2 ω  Vcell2

Eq. 1 of Holton & Frankel (2010): photons in a fully recorded spot from a crystal rotated through the reflection at angular speed ω. Mosaicity, divergence, bandwidth and mosaic-block size do not appear: they change the spot shape and the fraction of the spot recorded on a given frame (partiality), not the integrated intensity (§2.2 of that paper). Select a term to highlight the parameters that enter it.

Full-detector preview from eq. 1 with a Gaussian partiality and spot-shape model, binned 4 × 4 (300 µm display pixels, mean photons per 75 µm pixel). module gaps. Select a spot to run the nanoBragg kernel at native pixel size.

Model, assumptions and limits

Kernel. The zoom panel is a line-by-line JavaScript port of the nanoBragg pixel loop: for each pixel (and sub-pixel), source point, wavelength, φ step and mosaic domain it computes fractional h k l, the parallelepiped lattice transform sincg(πh,N)·sincg(πk,N)·sincg(πl,N), looks up |F| at the nearest integer hkl, and scales by re², fluence, pixel solid angle and the Kahn polarization factor. Source grids, dispersion steps and mosaic-domain generation follow the nanoBragg rules. Tested against the compiled program: spot sums agree within about ±15 % (different random mosaic domains), and for fully recorded reflections the kernel reproduces eq. 1 to 1.3 %.

Preview. The full-detector preview uses eq. 1 for the full spot, a Gaussian rocking profile (relp size, mosaic, divergence and bandwidth widths in quadrature) for partiality, and finite-difference Jacobians for spot shape. On 0.1° frames it overestimates partial spots by 0–50 % relative to the kernel, because the sinc² relp profile has wider tails than the Gaussian. Treat the kernel as the reference.

Stills. For a still, the time integral replaces L/ω: I = Ibeam t re² P A λ² (Vxtal/Vcell²) |F|² ρ(ε), with ρ the normalized rocking profile at excitation error ε. Integrating this over a rotation recovers eq. 1. This form is derived here, not quoted from the references.

Crystal. Structure factors are synthetic: a random-atom model with cubic-insulin composition (≈ 396 protein + 60 water atoms per asymmetric unit), I2₁3, a = 78.1 Å, B = 15 Å², Babinet bulk-solvent attenuation (k = 0.35, B = 46 Å²), computed with cctbx to 1.2 Å. Wilson statistics and systematic absences are realistic; individual |F| values are not those of insulin. The crystal is a cube of mosaic blocks of N³ unit cells; intensity scales with the number of blocks in the illuminated volume. Beam is a square top hat.

Not modelled. Detector quantum efficiency, sensor parallax and point-spread; crystal absorption beyond a single factor A; radiation damage; air scatter; the water-ring shape (nanoBragg's flat water model, F = 2.57, is used); intermodule geometry beyond the 12/38-pixel gaps.

  1. Holton, J. M. & Frankel, K. A. (2010). The minimum crystal size needed for a complete diffraction data set. Acta Cryst. D66, 393–408. doi:10.1107/S0907444910007262
  2. Holton, J. M., Classen, S., Frankel, K. A. & Tainer, J. A. (2014). The R-factor gap in macromolecular crystallography: an untapped potential for insights on accurate structures. FEBS J. 281, 4046–4060. doi:10.1111/febs.12922
  3. nanoBragg, J. M. Holton & K. A. Frankel; source nanoBragg_standalone.c in cctbx_project/simtbx/nanoBragg (github.com/cctbx/cctbx_project).
  4. Winter, G. et al. (2019). How best to use photons. Acta Cryst. D75, 242–261. doi:10.1107/S2059798319003528 (cubic insulin cell a ≈ 78.1 Å).
  5. DECTRIS EIGER2 X/XE specifications: 4148 × 4362 pixels, 75 µm, intermodule gaps 12/38 pixels, 450 µm Si.
